chunks: Al-Bazofari from Ahmad ibn Idris, from al-Husayn ibn Abi Abdillah ibn Abi al-Mughira, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Regarding a man who manumitted his slave conditionally (dabbara), and the slave ran away (abaq) and went to a people and married among them, without informing them that he was a slave. Children were born to him and he acquired wealth. Then the master who had manumitted him died. The heirs of the deceased master came and claimed the slave. I asked: What do you think? He said: 'The slave and his children belong to the heirs of the deceased master.' I said: 'Did he not manumit him?' He said: 'Indeed, when he ran away, he broke his manumission and returned to slavery.'

key_terms.أَبَقَ: To run away or escape from slavery
key_terms.تَدْبِير: The state of being a conditionally manumitted slave

ai.seo_question: What happens to a conditionally manumitted slave if he runs away before fulfilling the condition?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the legal mechanism of 'hdam al-tadbir' (annulment of manumission), establishing that a dabbir's flight (abaq) reverts him to full slavery, thereby keeping his children and acquired wealth under the ownership of the original master's heirs. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic view that conditional manumission is not absolute until the condition is met, and the slave's autonomy is contingent upon remaining within the master's domain.
